# Backpressure

Backpressure in a streaming pipeline is the mechanism by which a slow downstream consumer signals an upstream producer to reduce its emission rate, rather than letting an unbounded buffer grow until the process runs out of memory.

Without backpressure, a fast producer can overwhelm a slow consumer by continuously emitting data faster than the consumer can process it. This causes buffers to grow without bounds, eventually exhausting available memory and crashing the system.

## Common Implementations

The source describes three widely-used approaches:

**Bounded Queues**
Producers place items into a fixed-size queue. Once the queue reaches capacity, the producer blocks until the consumer removes items, creating a natural throttle on emission rate.

**Credit-Based Flow Control**
The consumer explicitly grants the producer permission to send N more items (a "credit"). The producer can only emit up to its current credit balance. As the consumer processes items, it grants additional credits, allowing the producer to continue at a controlled pace.

**Reactive-Pull Models**
Instead of the producer pushing items to the consumer, the consumer requests items on its own schedule. This inverts the control flow: the consumer only pulls data when it is ready to process it, naturally preventing overload.
